title: HE SENT AWAY TWO WOMEN… THEN HAD MORE CHILDREN. WHY DID GOD PRESERVE THIS FAMILY’S COMPLICATED STORY?
paragraphs: HE SENT AWAY TWO WOMEN… THEN HAD MORE CHILDREN. WHY DID GOD PRESERVE THIS FAMILY’S COMPLICATED STORY?

Buried in 1 Chronicles 8:8–11 is a family record filled with unanswered questions, broken relationships, and generations that continued after a painful separation. But the greatest surprise is not what Scripture reveals about Shaharaim. It is what this forgotten genealogy teaches us about the God who sees imperfect families—and the Savior who alone can redeem what sin has broken.
There are some family stories nobody wants to tell.
The marriage that ended.
The children who grew up wondering why someone left.
The parent whose name still brings silence to the dinner table.
The relationship everyone knows about but nobody discusses.
The painful decisions that divided one household into two.
And sometimes, years later, someone opens an old photograph, discovers a forgotten name, or hears a story that changes everything they thought they knew about their family.
Suddenly, the past doesn't feel so distant.
It feels personal.
Now imagine opening the Bible and discovering a family record that sounds uncomfortably familiar.
Not in the story of David and Bathsheba.
Not in the scandal surrounding Judah and Tamar.
Not even in the complicated household of Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar.
But in a genealogy most Christians have probably read past without stopping.
A few names.
A few children.
Two women who were sent away.
And one man whose household continued growing afterward.
His name was Shaharaim.
And although Scripture gives us only a handful of verses about him, those verses raise questions that reach straight into the complicated realities of family, responsibility, loss, and grace.
But before we go any further, there is something important we must understand.
The Bible does not tell us everything that happened in Shaharaim's household. And where God has not given us the details, we must not pretend that we know them.
That restraint matters.
Because sometimes the most faithful way to read Scripture is not to invent a scandal.
It is to recognize the pain that might surround a story while allowing God's Word to speak for itself.
And what His Word actually says is remarkable enough.
In 1 Chronicles 8:8–11, we read:

"And Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives. And he begat of Hodesh his wife, Jobab, and Zibia, and Mesha, and Malcham, And Jeuz, and Shachia, and Mirma. These were his sons, heads of the fathers. And of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal."
— 1 Chronicles 8:8–11, King James Version
Read those verses again.
Slowly.
Shaharaim had children in Moab after sending away Hushim and Baara, who are identified as his wives.
The record then names Hodesh as another wife and lists children associated with her.
And afterward, it names two sons born to Hushim.
There is no dramatic speech.
No explanation of why the women were sent away.
No recorded conversation.
No account of tears, confrontation, repentance, reconciliation, or judgment.
Just a family record preserved in the Word of God.
And perhaps that is what makes this passage so unsettling.
We want Scripture to explain every broken relationship. Sometimes Scripture records the relationship without explaining the wound.
We want to know who was right.
Who was wrong.
Who suffered.
Who walked away.
Who tried to make things right.
But the passage does not answer those questions.
And the silence forces us to confront something uncomfortable.
Not every family story comes with an explanation.
Not every question receives an answer in this life.
And not every person carrying the consequences of someone else's decisions gets to hear the apology they deserved.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe you grew up in a household where adults made decisions you were too young to understand.
Maybe your family has names that are rarely mentioned.
Maybe you watched someone leave and spent years wondering whether you were the reason.
Or perhaps you are the one who made the decision.
The one who walked away.
The one who damaged trust.
The one who now looks back at a complicated family history and wonders whether God can still work through a life filled with regret.
If that is you, stay with this story.
Because there is a difference between a Bible passage describing human behavior and God approving that behavior.
And understanding that difference can change how we read not only Shaharaim's story, but our own.
The original Hebrew makes this passage especially interesting.
In 1 Chronicles 8:8, the phrase commonly translated "after he had sent them away" includes the Hebrew expression:
אַחֲרֵי שִׁלְּחוֹ אֹתָם
'aḥărê shilleḥô 'ōtām
The expression communicates the idea of "after his sending them away."
The verb comes from the Hebrew root שָׁלַח (shalach), meaning "to send," "send away," or "release," depending on context.
That is significant.
Because the passage describes a sending away, but it does not provide a complete legal or emotional account of what happened.
Some English translations render the situation differently because the Hebrew wording and relationships in this genealogy are difficult to interpret.
The identity of Hodesh is also discussed by interpreters, and the relationship between the names Hodesh and Baara is not explained with enough clarity to settle every question confidently.
The Hebrew text identifies Hushim and Baara as wives, while verse 9 refers to Hodesh as a wife.
That is what we can say.
What we cannot responsibly say is that Shaharaim definitely committed a particular act of cruelty, that either woman was guilty of wrongdoing, or that we know the motives behind the separation.
Scripture does not tell us.
And this is where biblical interpretation demands humility.
We must never turn the Bible's silence into permission to manufacture accusations.
But neither should we miss the larger reality.
This was a complicated family record.
And God allowed it to remain in Scripture.
Why?
To answer that, we need to remember what Chronicles is doing.
The opening chapters of 1 Chronicles preserve genealogies connecting Israel's families, tribes, settlements, and history.
These records mattered because God's covenant dealings unfolded through real people across real generations.
The names were not decorative.
They connected people to their ancestry and to the unfolding history of Israel.
Shaharaim's descendants belonged to that historical record.
Their existence mattered.
Their names mattered.
And their family history was not erased simply because its details were complicated.
Think about that.
God's Word contains genealogies that do not hide the existence of imperfect human households.
But we must be careful about what this means.
Being named in Scripture is not proof that every action a person took pleased God.
The Bible records murderers, adulterers, idolaters, deceivers, and unfaithful rulers.
Their inclusion does not equal divine approval.
The Bible is not a collection of flawless families. It is the truthful record of God's dealings with a fallen world.
And that truth becomes even clearer when we look at the broader biblical story.
Abraham's household experienced painful conflict involving Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob's family was marked by rivalry, favoritism, and jealousy.
David's household suffered devastating consequences from sin.
Yet the Bible does not present those failures as virtues.
It exposes human weakness while revealing the faithfulness of God.
And ultimately, Scripture directs our attention beyond every flawed household toward the One who came to redeem sinners.
Jesus Christ.
But before we reach the cross, we need to face another uncomfortable truth.
Sometimes people use the language of grace to avoid the responsibility of repentance.
They say, "God knows my heart."
And He does.
They say, "Nobody is perfect."
And that is true.
They say, "God can use anyone."
And Scripture certainly demonstrates His power to accomplish His purposes despite human failure.
But none of those statements makes wrongdoing acceptable.
Grace is not permission to abandon responsibility.
Forgiveness is not an excuse to continue harming people.
And God's sovereignty does not transform every human decision into a righteous one.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts that misunderstanding directly:
"What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?"
God's grace does not invite us to become comfortable with sin.
It calls us to turn away from it.
That matters for anyone reading this who has wounded a spouse, neglected a child, betrayed a family member, or refused to acknowledge the damage caused by personal choices.
You may not be able to rewrite yesterday.
But repentance can change how you live today.
You can tell the truth.
You can stop defending what was wrong.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can take responsibility where responsibility belongs.
You can make restitution where possible.
You can respect the boundaries of people you have hurt.
And you can begin walking in obedience even when reconciliation is not immediately possible.
Because repentance is more than feeling terrible about the past.
The Greek word commonly translated "repent" is μετανοέω (metanoeō), carrying the sense of changing one's mind or turning in response to God's truth.
Biblical repentance is not merely emotional regret.
It involves a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in changed conduct.
Jesus said in Luke 13:3:
"Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish."
Those are serious words.
And they remind us that the deepest problem in every human story is not simply a damaged reputation or a complicated family background.
It is sin.
Sin separates us from the holy God who created us.
Sin distorts love.
Sin corrupts motives.
Sin wounds relationships.
Sin convinces us that our desires matter more than God's commands.
And sometimes sin leaves consequences that continue long after the moment of disobedience has passed.
But there is another danger.
It is possible to carry shame for sins you did not commit.
Maybe someone abandoned your family.
Maybe you were born into a complicated relationship.
Maybe you grew up feeling that your very existence was an embarrassment.
Maybe people treated you as though the circumstances surrounding your birth determined your worth.
Hear this carefully.
You are not morally guilty simply because someone else made sinful decisions before you were born.
Ezekiel 18:20 declares:
"The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son."
Each person is accountable before God for their own sin.
And no child should be treated as though their life is a mistake simply because the adults around them failed.
That does not mean our backgrounds have no consequences.
They can shape our fears, relationships, memories, and struggles.
But they do not determine whether we are beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Perhaps this is the part of the story you needed most.
Because for years, you have been carrying a question you never dared to ask aloud.
"Am I less worthy because of where I came from?"
No.
Your family history may explain part of your pain.
It does not establish your value before God.
You were made in His image.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not restricted to people with respectable family backgrounds.
It is extended to sinners who need a Savior.
Which brings us to something extraordinary.
When the New Testament opens with the genealogy of Jesus Christ in Matthew 1, it does not present a family history carefully edited to avoid every uncomfortable name.
It includes Judah and Tamar.
It mentions Rahab.
It remembers Ruth, a Moabite woman.
It refers to David and "her that had been the wife of Urias."
These references carry histories of vulnerability, sin, loss, redemption, and God's providential faithfulness.
Their stories are not identical.
Their moral circumstances must not be confused.
And their inclusion should not be used to excuse wrongdoing.
But together, they remind us that God's redemptive plan was never dependent on humanity producing a spotless ancestral record.
Jesus entered the world through a real human family history.
Yet He Himself was without sin.
Hebrews 4:15 says that He was:
"in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin."
That distinction is everything.
Jesus did not come because human families were already righteous.
He came because humanity needed redemption.
He did not enter history to celebrate sin.
He entered history to defeat it.
He did not suffer on the cross merely to improve our self-image.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
And this is where the story moves from an ancient genealogy into the deepest question of your own life.
What will you do with Jesus?
Not simply what will you do with your family history.
Not simply how will you explain your mistakes.
Not simply how will you survive the consequences of someone else's choices.
But what will you do with the Savior who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His death and resurrection?
Because the Gospel is greater than a motivational promise that everything will eventually feel better.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day.
That is the message of 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
The Greek word χάρις (charis), commonly translated "grace," speaks of favor or gift, and in the New Testament it powerfully expresses God's undeserved favor toward sinners.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
Notice what that means.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot inherit salvation from a respectable family name.
You cannot earn acceptance with God by building a religious reputation.
And you cannot make yourself righteous by pretending your past never happened.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.
Received by faith.
Not earned through human achievement.
Not bought through religious payments.
Not secured by public approval.
And that truth is liberating.
Because some people spend their entire lives trying to become worthy of love by hiding the very things they are ashamed of.
They smile in church.
They post encouraging verses.
They tell everyone they are doing fine.
But privately, they are still grieving the home they never had.
Still replaying the words that destroyed their confidence.
Still struggling to forgive.
Still haunted by what they did.
Still wondering whether the person they used to be has permanently disqualified them from becoming someone different.
And maybe tonight, while reading this, you recognize yourself.
You have become very good at looking healed.
But you know there are places in your heart where the pain is still real.
You know the memories you avoid.
The conversations you rehearse.
The prayers you start but cannot finish.
The names that still make your chest tighten.
And perhaps you have been asking God why He has not simply erased everything.
But Scripture does not promise that conversion will erase every painful memory or remove every earthly consequence.
It promises something deeper.
A new relationship with God through Christ.
A new identity in Him.
The indwelling work of the Holy Spirit.
The call and power to walk in newness of life.
And the sure hope that God will ultimately make all things new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
That does not mean every broken relationship is instantly repaired.
It means belonging to Christ changes the deepest reality of who you are and the direction of your life.
Your past may still have consequences.
But your past does not have to remain your master.
Your failures may still require accountability.
But your failures do not have to be your final identity.
Your family may have handed you painful memories.
But through Christ, you can begin building a different legacy.
One marked by truth instead of secrecy.
Faithfulness instead of betrayal.
Humility instead of pride.
Repentance instead of excuses.
And grace instead of bitterness.
This is why we must resist the temptation to reduce Shaharaim's record to a sensational story about a man and multiple women.
The passage does not tell us whether Shaharaim repented of anything.
It does not tell us whether Hushim or Baara were mistreated.
It does not tell us how the children experienced their household.
It does not tell us whether reconciliation ever happened.
And it certainly does not tell us that Shaharaim's life is a model for Christian marriage.
But it does remind us that Scripture preserves the names of real families living in a world where human relationships were not always simple.
And when we read that record in the light of the whole Bible, we are led to a greater truth.
The hope of humanity is not found in having an uncomplicated genealogy.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
And if that truth is beginning to reach somewhere deep inside you, do not rush past it.
Ask yourself something.
Have you been blaming your past for a sin God is calling you to repent of?
Or have you been blaming yourself for a wound someone else caused?
Those are two very different burdens.
And they require different responses.
If you have sinned, do not hide behind your circumstances.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
Seek His mercy through Christ.
Begin making the changes that genuine repentance requires.
But if you have been carrying shame for another person's wrongdoing, do not continue treating yourself as though you are guilty simply because you were hurt.
Bring that burden to Jesus.
Seek wise, trustworthy support where needed.
Learn to distinguish forgiveness from pretending harm never happened.
And remember that setting appropriate boundaries is not the same as refusing to forgive.
You can pursue healing without denying the truth.
You can honor God without calling evil good.
You can release vengeance to the Lord without placing yourself back into an unsafe situation.
And you can trust Christ even when some questions remain unanswered.
That is not weak faith.
Sometimes that is what faithful endurance looks like.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy would be to read this passage, become fascinated by Shaharaim's complicated household, and never examine the condition of our own hearts.
Because the question is not merely, "What happened to those women?"
It is also, "What is happening in me?"
Am I telling the truth about my life?
Am I honoring my commitments?
Am I taking responsibility for my actions?
Am I treating people as image-bearers of God rather than disposable parts of my story?
Am I seeking forgiveness where I have done wrong?
Am I allowing bitterness to harden my heart?
Am I following Jesus—or merely using His name to make myself feel better about decisions I refuse to surrender?
These are not comfortable questions.
But sometimes the questions that disturb us most are the ones we most need to bring before God.
And if this article has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to turn the comment section into a public confession of private details.
You do not have to explain everything.
Sometimes a few honest words can help another struggling believer realize they are not alone.
But remember: a comment is not repentance, and a public declaration is not a substitute for faith in Christ.
What matters most is the response of your heart before God.
And maybe there is someone else who needs this truth.
A single parent exhausted from trying to hold a family together.
An adult child still grieving abandonment.
A husband or wife struggling with the consequences of betrayal.
A believer ashamed of a past relationship.
A young person who thinks their family background makes them spiritually inferior.
Or someone who has spent years assuming that God only works through people with beautiful stories.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
But because someone scrolling silently may encounter a passage of Scripture they have never considered and be reminded of the grace offered through Jesus Christ.
Because there may come a night when you need to remember that the Gospel is not reserved for people whose families have never fallen apart.
It is good news for sinners who come to the Savior.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn Scripture into entertainment.
Not to sensationalize ancient stories.
Not to promise that faith will eliminate every earthly struggle.
But to help people encounter biblical truth, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and follow Jesus with greater faithfulness.
And if this ministry has been helping you grow, I want to invite you into something more than simply reading another article.
Help us continue bringing Christ-centered biblical teaching to people who are hungry for God's Word.
Following Gospel Warrior allows you to stay connected with regular Scripture reflections, biblical encouragement, conviction, and discipleship resources.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment more accessible.
Think of it as a voluntary ministry offering—a tangible expression of generosity toward work you believe is worth supporting.
But let us be biblically clear.
Biblical giving should be voluntary, thoughtful, and sincere.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
If you belong to a local church, do not neglect your responsibilities there in order to support an online ministry.
It is not.
These are simply expressions of appreciation—not spiritual rewards, and certainly not substitutes for the eternal treasure found in Christ.
Keep testing what you read against Scripture.
Keep seeking Christ.
Keep growing in truth.
Because a ministry should never become the center of your faith.
Jesus must remain the center.
Always.
Now, return with me for one final moment to that ancient family record.
Shaharaim.
Hushim.
Baara.
Hodesh.
Jobab.
Zibia.
Mesha.
Malcham.
Jeuz.
Shachia.
Mirma.
Abitub.
Elpaal.
Names most people will never remember.
Lives separated from us by thousands of years.
A family record with questions Scripture does not answer.
Yet those names remain in the biblical text.
And here we are, centuries later, reading them.
Not because we know everything about their lives.
Not because their household was necessarily an example to imitate.
But because God's Word has preserved a historical record that reminds us how real and complicated human history can be.
And now you must consider your own story.
One day, the conversations you had, the decisions you made, the people you loved, and the responsibilities you carried will become part of the past.
Your descendants may never know all your struggles.
They may not understand every decision.
They may inherit consequences you never intended.
But today, while you still have breath, you have an opportunity to respond to God.
To repent where you have sinned.
To seek reconciliation where it is right and possible.
To care for those entrusted to you.
To stop repeating patterns of harm.
To speak truth where silence has protected wrongdoing.
To extend forgiveness without abandoning wisdom.
And above all, to put your faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Because no matter how complicated your family history may be, the most important question is not whether your ancestors lived perfectly.
It is whether you have been reconciled to God through His Son.
The Bible does not promise that every scandal becomes a beautiful earthly ending.
But it does proclaim a Savior who died for sinners and rose victorious from the grave.
A Savior whose grace is greater than the guilt of those who truly turn to Him.
A Savior who does not need us to falsify the past in order to give us hope for the future.
That is why our message remains:
Not because scandal is good.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because consequences disappear.
But because Jesus Christ offers real forgiveness, real redemption, and real transformation to those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
Pray.
Examine your heart.
And ask the Lord what obedience looks like for you today.
And remember this:
You cannot change the names written in your family's past, but by God's grace, you can choose whom you will follow with the life still ahead of you.
